questions.q: Why is df["quantity"] * df["unit_price"] preferred over .apply() for computing a line_total column?
options: It's a vectorized operation — faster and more concise than calling a function row by row for simple arithmetic
.apply() cannot perform multiplication under any circumstances
They produce different results, so .apply() is actually required here
Vectorized operations only work on string columns
questions.explain: Vectorized operations let pandas/NumPy apply the operation to the whole column at once.

questions.q: In this lesson's order_size example, how many of the 20 orders in orders.csv are classified "Large" (line_total >= 200)?
questions.explain: Orders 1001, 1002, 1009, 1013, 1015, and 1020 each have a line_total of $249.50 or more.

questions.q: What does df["quantity"].clip(lower=0) do to order 1014's quantity of -1?
options: Replaces it with 0, since it's below the specified lower bound
Converts it to a missing value (NaN)
questions.explain: clip(lower=0) replaces any value below 0 with 0, leaving every other value untouched.

questions.q: Why didn't clipping quantity after computing line_total change line_total for order 1014 in this lesson's example?
options: line_total was already computed from the original, unclipped quantity value — order of operations matters
line_total is recalculated automatically whenever quantity changes
Order 1014 doesn't have a line_total value
clip() always updates every other derived column automatically
questions.explain: A real pipeline should clean or clip a column before deriving new columns from it, not after.

questions.q: What does the .str accessor let you do on a pandas column?
options: Apply ordinary string methods like .upper() or .contains() across the entire column at once
Convert any column to a string type permanently
Only works on columns with fewer than 10 unique values
Count the number of missing values in a column
questions.explain: df["region"].str.upper() is the vectorized equivalent of calling .upper() on every value in a loop.
